sections.title: React can own one region
sections.body: An existing site does not need a full rewrite. Add a DOM container where an interactive feature belongs, create a React root for that container, and render a component into it. The rest of the page can remain server-rendered HTML or use another stack. This limits migration risk and lets the team learn from one real feature.

sections.title: The existing build comes first
sections.body: If the project already supports modules, npm packages, and JSX transformation, integrate React into that setup instead of creating a second unrelated toolchain. Install react and react-dom, confirm JSX support, and follow the backend or framework’s asset pipeline. If no modular environment exists, React’s guide points to Vite and its backend integrations as one option.

sections.title: The container defines React ownership
sections.body:
Add a stable unique element such as
to the existing HTML. Find it after it exists, call createRoot(container), then root.render(). React manages the DOM inside that container. Existing HTML outside it remains owned by the existing page. A missing or mistyped ID makes the container null and prevents rendering.

sections.title: Several islands are possible
sections.body: A partly React page can have separate roots for unrelated regions. Each root has its own component tree, so shared state and coordinated updates need an explicit design. If the host page removes a React-owned region, call root.unmount first so React can clean up subscriptions and other resources. Server-rendered React markup needs hydrateRoot rather than createRoot.

sections.title: Use evidence instead of setup guesses
sections.body: When setup fails, identify the layer before changing code. Read the terminal command and first error, confirm the current directory and versions, check the browser Network and Console, and trace the entry file to the root component. Make one small correction, rerun the same check, and record what proved the fix.

interviewQuestions.question: What responsibility does adding react to an existing page have in a React project?
interviewQuestions.answer: Explain gradual React adoption. Reuse or add a modular JavaScript environment. Connect a stable DOM node with createRoot. Use multiple roots deliberately and clean them up.
interviewQuestions.followUp: What important responsibility belongs to another layer?

interviewQuestions.question: How would you debug a failure related to adding react to an existing page?
interviewQuestions.answer: Reproduce the smallest failure, confirm the current directory and versions when relevant, read the first terminal or browser error, trace the entry and root, and test one hypothesis at a time.
interviewQuestions.followUp: Which evidence would make you change layers?

interviewQuestions.question: Which tradeoff in adding react to an existing page should a team decide explicitly?
interviewQuestions.answer: The team should match tools and boundaries to product needs, record version and deployment assumptions, and avoid treating a starter template as a complete production architecture.
interviewQuestions.followUp: How could the answer change for an existing server-rendered site?

commonMistakes.symptom: Every setup problem is described as a React error.
commonMistakes.cause: Browser, Node, npm, Vite, project files, and React responsibilities were mixed together.
commonMistakes.fix: Identify the failing layer from the command, URL, stack, file, or tool panel before editing.

commonMistakes.symptom: Commands work in one terminal but fail in another folder.
commonMistakes.cause: The current directory or active Node installation differs.
commonMistakes.fix: Check the path, package.json, lockfile, node -v, and npm -v in the same terminal.

commonMistakes.symptom: The starter template is treated as a complete production plan.
commonMistakes.cause: Scaffolding and build features were confused with routing, data, server, security, and deployment architecture.
commonMistakes.fix: Write product requirements and assign each responsibility to React, a build tool, a framework, the platform, or backend code.
